extracted.intended_audience: instructors/teachers of discrete mathematics (secondary or undergraduate) preparing classroom activities on polyhedra and Euler's formula
extracted.subtask_description: Classroom-tested, discovery-based activities and instructor notes for guiding students to discover and prove Euler's formula (and generalizations) by constructing polyhedra, measuring vertices/edges/faces, making conjectures, and using combinatorial and inductive proofs. Includes definitions, worksheets, proofs, and extensions (angle deficiency, higher genus/Poincaré).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of polyhedron (working definition used)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polyhedra are defined as embedded compact two-dimensional polygonal surfaces with planar, nonself-intersecting faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes some authors drop some of these criteria (e.g., Kepler–Poinsot polyhedra have self-intersecting faces), but the stricter definition is used here to avoid complications in classroom activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's formula — polyhedral version
rubrics_metrics.description: For any polyhedron topologically equivalent to a sphere with V vertices, E edges and F faces, V - E + F = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number of faces F includes the outside (unbounded) face in planar embeddings. The hypothesis 'topologically equivalent to a sphere' is necessary; nonspherical (e.g., toroidal) polyhedra do not generally satisfy the formula without modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's formula — graph version
rubrics_metrics.description: For any connected simple plane graph with V vertices, E edges and F faces (regions), V - E + F = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple = no loops or multiple edges, plane = embedded without crossing edges. The simple-graph assumption simplifies the inductive proof, but the result can be extended beyond simple graphs. This graph version is the basis for a classroom inductive proof of Euler's formula for polyhedra (via Schlegel diagrams or flattening).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery-based Polyhedra Exploration activity requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Students build physical models of various polyhedra from given polygon pieces, then collect data (V, E, F) and make conjectures about relationships among these numbers (leading to Euler's formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works best with many Polydrons or GeoFix shapes; can take as little as 20 minutes with ready materials. Worksheets and solutions are provided. Instructor should demonstrate one model (tetrahedron) and randomly assign assemblies via cards or numbers. Early finishers get additional assembly problems or second items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials and construction constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When using homemade polygons, every side length must be the same for all polygons; recommended minimum counts of polygons for classroom use are provided (e.g., 76 triangles, 29 squares, 14 pentagons, 20 hexagons, 6 octagons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative materials (tape and cardstock) increase assembly time. If planning to include additional assembly problems, additional counts (e.g., at least 30 more triangles, 18 more squares, 34 more pentagons) are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional assembly open-ended problems (pedagogical target)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary construction challenges (e.g., 'Using only triangles, make two distinct polyhedra', 'Make a polyhedron using as many different shapes as you can') meant to generate many distinct examples and stimulate creative exploration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most are open-ended (except the snub cube example). Warn instructors to watch for students who create toroidal (nonspherical) polyhedra, which violate Euler's basic formulation and are useful teachable counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning objective: practice making conjectures and choosing propositions to prove
rubrics_metrics.description: One important instructional goal is having students formulate conjectures (e.g., relationships among V, E, F) and then identify appropriate propositions to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This activity prepares students for subsequent presentation of proofs (like induction on number of edges). Emphasize determination of the correct proposition to prove as a key proof-writing skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor facilitation strategy for discovery activities
rubrics_metrics.description: During discovery tasks, instructors should wait a long time for student suggestions, steer as little as possible, and avoid giving hints. When students create informal definitions, the instructor may refine them but should not prematurely supply labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit the depth and precision of definitions to course needs. Avoid rejecting examples or defining concepts in a way that later prevents discussion of student-generated examples. Encourage creativity and broad thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class management logistics for activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical notes on running activities: assign items individually or in groups, use half-sheets/index cards for assignment, handle early finishers by assigning additional tasks, and collect completed tables for class conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a completed table (solutions) for reference. Use group randomness to vary student experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some of these things are not like the others (sorting/activity rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students sort a collection of polyhedral models into two piles based on whether they possess a chosen property, then articulate those distinguishing features and appropriate vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This activity targets pattern recognition, geometric reasoning, hypothesis testing, and nomenclature development. Instructor should withhold formal vocabulary until students have described the property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Regular Polyhedron / Platonic Solid
rubrics_metrics.description: For convex polyhedra: all faces are regular polygons of exactly one type and each vertex has the same number of polygons around it; modern definition is 'flag transitive' (any two incident vertex-edge-face flags can be mapped by symmetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note combinatorial exceptions (a nonconvex combinatorial polyhedron satisfying isogonal/isotoxal/isohedral but not modern regularity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Convex polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron is convex if every pair of points on or in the polyhedron determines a segment contained entirely in or on the polyhedron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loosely described to mean 'lacks dents.' Convex polyhedra are spherical, so Euler applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Symmetric polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: Any polyhedron with a nontrivial symmetry mapping the polyhedron to itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used informally to motivate discussion of isogonality, isohedrality, isotoxality and uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Isogonal polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: Any vertex may be mapped to any other vertex by a symmetry of the polyhedron (vertex-transitive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: triangular prism is isogonal; square pyramid is not (apex distinct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Isohedral polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: Any face may be mapped to any other face by a symmetry of the polyhedron (face-transitive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: triangular bipyramid is isohedral; Archimedean solids are not necessarily isohedral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Isotoxal polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: Any edge may be mapped to any other edge by a symmetry of the polyhedron (edge-transitive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: cuboctahedron is isotoxal; triangular bipyramid is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Uniform (semiregular) polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: An isogonal polyhedron in which all faces are regular polygons (not necessarily congruent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used synonymously with Archimedean in many sources, but distinctions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Vertex star (notation and usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The collection of polygons incident to a vertex; described combinatorially as a cyclic list of numbers (counts of sides) separated by periods, e.g., (5.6.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single vertex-star sequence can characterize a uniform polyhedron and is useful for cataloguing symmetric polyhedra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Archimedean polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron in which all vertex stars are congruent and the faces are all regular polygons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes conflated with 'uniform'; examples and exceptions are discussed in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Prism
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron with two parallel congruent faces connected by parallelograms; a right prism has rectangles as lateral faces; if those rectangles are squares and parallel polygons are regular, the prism is uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when constructing or classifying student-built models in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Antiprism
rubrics_metrics.description: A convex uniform polyhedron with two parallel congruent regular n-gons and 2n equilateral triangles forming a strip connecting them; vertex stars are of type (3.3.3...n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in classifying constructions and in Exercise 6 as examples completing classification tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Spherical polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron topologically equivalent to a sphere (i.e., genus g = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euler's formula applies directly to spherical polyhedra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Toroidal polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron topologically equivalent to a torus (genus g = 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provide counterexamples to naive Euler formula and motivate Poincaré's generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Simple polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron in which each vertex has degree 3 (three edges meeting at each vertex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'simple' can vary in usage; authors clarify that some use it differently (e.g., spherical simple). Simple ↔ dual of simplicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Simplicial polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: A polyhedron composed entirely of triangular faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dual of a simplicial polyhedron is simple and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric Polyhedra & Angle Deficiency activity requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Students build/flatten vertex stars, measure angle deficiency at vertices (2π minus sum of incident angles), compute total angle deficiency, and conjecture/prove relationships (e.g., total deficiency relates to Euler characteristic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use radians; interior angle of regular n-gon is π( n-2 )/n = (n-2)π/n or as given (π(n-2)/n). Exercises guide students to compute deficiencies, fill tables of vertex symbols, and derive total angle deficiency via counting two ways and Euler's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical emphasis: counting arguments (proofs by counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use counting the same quantity two ways (edges around faces vs edges around vertices, etc.) as a central combinatorial proof technique, including in the proofs of Euler-based theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5 and Appendix B examples demonstrate and provide exercises for proofs by counting; instructors should highlight this method as a major theme in discrete mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive proof guideline (Appendix A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove Euler's formula for connected simple plane graphs by strong induction on number of edges: base case E=0 or 1, then remove an edge and consider two cases (remaining graph connected or split into two components), applying the induction hypothesis to obtain V - E + F = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain relation between polyhedra and plane graphs via Schlegel diagram or balloon-flattening. Emphasize the two-case analysis on removing an edge: face-splitting vs component-splitting, and how V,E,F change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: proving there are only five regular convex polyhedra
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Euler's theorem and inequalities from counting edges around faces and vertices, derive a constraint 1/k + 1/d > 1/2 for face-size k and vertex-degree d, yielding only five admissible pairs (Platonic solids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should demonstrate counting edges by faces (Fk = 2E) and by vertices (Vd = 2E) then substitute into Euler to derive constraints; use models to show existence of the five cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: lower bound on pentagons in polyhedra with all faces having ≥5 sides
rubrics_metrics.description: For any polyhedron made entirely of polygons with five or more sides, there must be at least 12 pentagons (counting faces f_n and using Euler and degree constraints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by expressing F = sum f_n, using 2E = sum n f_n and 3V ≤ 2E, and manipulating inequalities to conclude f5 ≥ 12. Simplify for classroom by restricting face types to pentagons and hexagons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: fullerenes — pentagon count fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Any simple polyhedron composed only of pentagons and hexagons (a fullerene) must have exactly 12 pentagons; the number of hexagons is unconstrained by Euler alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses angle deficiency or counting; mention chemical relevance (C60 buckminsterfullerene) and that non-simple/nonregular faces can break the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global combinatorial identity for simple polyhedra
rubrics_metrics.description: Every simple polyhedron satisfies the equality sum_{n>=3} (6 - n) f_n = 12 (or an equivalent form), which is useful for constraints on face counts under face-type restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this identity to deduce results like presence of faces with ≤5 sides or uniqueness of cube for quadrangulations; show how pentagon/heptagon counts differ by 12 in mixed examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré generalization activity (higher genus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students construct toroidal polyhedra (donuts), count V,E,F and observe Euler's formula fails; introduce genus g and Poincaré formula V - E + F = 2 - 2g, then use templates to build n-holed tori and predict counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet guides students through constructing 1-, 2-, 3-holed tori and counting, then generalizing to n-holed surfaces. Use gluing of faces/rectangles to demonstrate how genus affects Euler characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worksheet completion & assessment criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must complete worksheets: record V, E, F for constructed polyhedra, compute sums like V+F, and observe/verify Euler's formula or Poincaré generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solutions and completed tables are provided for instructor reference. Instructors can assess understanding by whether students correctly count V,E,F, notice the invariant V - E + F (or its genus-generalization), and can explain deviations for nonspherical examples.
